sections.overview: The dugong is a fully marine sirenian and the only living member of Dugongidae. It ranges through tropical coastal waters from East Africa and the Red Sea across the Indian Ocean to the western Pacific, where seagrass grows. Unlike manatees, some of which enter rivers, the dugong has a notched tail fluke rather than a rounded paddle. Its life follows shallow seagrass beds: it feeds and rests nearby, and moves when food patches shift or deteriorate.
sections.identification: An adult has a heavy, tapered body, short foreflippers and no visible hind limbs. Its broad muzzle turns down toward the seabed; a flexible upper lip and sensory bristles help it find and pull plants. Sparse hair covers the grey skin, which can look brown or green where algae grow. The tail has two pointed lobes. Males may develop small tusks from their upper incisors. Together, the downturned muzzle and fluked tail distinguish the dugong from manatees and suit a slow-swimming grazer of the seabed. Adults are around three metres long and may weigh up to 500 kilograms.
sections.habitat: Dugongs favour warm, shallow coastal waters with seagrass, especially protected bays, lagoons, channels and island shores. Most feeding occurs in shallow water, often less than 20 metres deep, though animals also use deeper meadows over broad, gently sloping shelves. Seagrass beds are patchy and vary in species, quality and seasonal growth. Tracking in Queensland and the Northern Territory found both relatively local animals and individuals travelling hundreds of kilometres. Movement is individual and food-linked; it is not one fixed migration route shared by all dugongs.
sections.diet: Seagrasses make up nearly all of the dugong’s diet. Its muzzle and bristled upper lip help it pull shoots from the sediment. Where plants can be uprooted, dugongs may eat leaves, rhizomes and roots; on firm ground or among resistant plants, they crop leaves instead. Root feeding is therefore conditional, not universal. At Ambon, Indonesia, field researchers recorded dugongs removing shoots and below-ground biomass from Halodule uninervis beds. Dugongs often select digestible, nutrient-rich species. Their trails through soft sediment show where grazing has disturbed the meadow.
sections.behavior: Dugongs breathe air and surface between bouts of underwater feeding. They occur alone, in small groups or in larger feeding aggregations. Observations in Moreton Bay, Australia, found that animals in dense herds spent more time feeding, suggesting that food helped bring them together. Neighbours changed frequently, and the herds were not clearly organized as protection against predators. Mothers and calves remain close; calves sometimes travel or rest over their mothers’ backs. The same observations showed that mother–calf pairs spent more time near the surface than lone animals, increasing their exposure to boat strikes. These findings describe that bay rather than every dugong population.
sections.reproduction: Dugongs mature late and usually produce one calf after a pregnancy estimated at about fourteen months. Births are separated by several years, with longer intervals when food is poor, so populations replace lost adults slowly. The calf is born underwater. It nurses while also beginning to eat seagrass soon after birth. It remains close to her for roughly one or two years. Age at first birth and birth intervals vary among populations. In Torres Strait, reproduction was lower during a period of seagrass decline than when meadows were abundant, although food and population density could not be separated as causes.
sections.ecology: As a large herbivore, the dugong changes the meadows where it feeds. Cropping leaves or excavating plants creates trails and alters the balance between shoots and underground parts. At one Indonesian site, grazing removed much of the shoots and upper below-ground biomass; tracks recovered during wet-season growth but not in the dry season. Effects are thus local and seasonal. Grazing produces a shifting pattern of cropped and intact patches, while seagrass meadows also shelter young fish and invertebrates. Dugong health and meadow condition are closely connected.
sections.conservation: The amended global IUCN assessment of 2015, published in 2019, classifies the dugong as Vulnerable. Separate 2022 assessments classify the East African subpopulation as Critically Endangered and New Caledonia’s as Endangered. Those categories apply locally, not to the whole species. Fishing nets can entangle and drown dugongs; hunting, boat strikes, and seagrass loss or degradation add pressure. East Africa’s assessment reports very low numbers and fishing deaths. In New Caledonia, hunting and boat injuries combine with seagrass decline linked to coastal development, pollution and anchoring. Slow maturity and infrequent births impede recovery after adult losses.
